question: In the later Vedic period, the 'Rajasuya' sacrifice performed by a king signified ______.
option_1: the settlement of a boundary dispute with a neighbour
option_2: the beginning of the agricultural season
option_3: the founding of a new capital city
option_4: his consecration and the assertion of his sovereignty
solution_text:
The correct answer is his consecration and the assertion of his sovereignty.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Rajasuya was the great royal consecration sacrifice of the later Vedic period. It was performed at the accession of a king and was believed to confer supreme power and sovereignty upon him. (राजसूय यज्ञ — राज्याभिषेक एवं संप्रभुता)

 

• The major sacrifices of the period, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Rajasuya — the coronation sacrifice, conferring sovereignty
◦ Ashvamedha — the horse sacrifice; a horse was set free to wander for a year, and all the territory it traversed unchallenged was claimed by the king
◦ Vajapeya — a chariot race against the king's kinsmen, which the king was required to win, symbolising supremacy over his clan
◦ Agnistoma — a soma sacrifice offered to Agni
◦ Hiranyagarbha — a ritual of rebirth through a golden vessel, performed with the assistance of the Brahmanas

 

• These sacrifices were conducted by the Brahmanas, who received rich gifts (dakshina) for them, and they mark the growing power of both the king and the priesthood in the later Vedic age.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four Vedas are the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Yajurveda deals specifically with the rituals and procedures of sacrifice, and is recited by the Adhvaryu priest.

 

• The four principal priests of a great sacrifice were the Hotri (Rigveda), Udgatri (Samaveda), Adhvaryu (Yajurveda) and Brahma (Atharvaveda).

 

• Later Vedic political terms: Samrat, Ekrat, Virat and Bhoja for kings of varying rank, and Sabha and Samiti for the assemblies.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 describes agricultural rites, of which the Vedic texts mention several, but not the Rajasuya.

 

• Option 3 and Option 1 describe events that were never marked by this sacrifice; the Rajasuya was concerned exclusively with kingship.

question: The Second Five Year Plan of India laid its principal emphasis on which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Heavy and basic industries.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961) laid its principal emphasis on the development of heavy and basic industries, in order to build a self-reliant industrial base. (द्वितीय पंचवर्षीय योजना — भारी एवं आधारभूत उद्योग)

 

• It was based on the P.C. Mahalanobis model and is therefore also called the Nehru-Mahalanobis Plan. The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, which classified industries into three schedules and gave the public sector the commanding heights of the economy, belongs to this plan.

 

• Three great steel plants were set up during this period with foreign collaboration — Bhilai (Soviet Union), Rourkela (West Germany) and Durgapur (United Kingdom). The Atomic Energy Commission and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research were also strengthened in this period.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The emphasis of the other plans:
◦ First (1951-56) — agriculture and irrigation; based on the Harrod-Domar model; the most successful plan
◦ Third (1961-66) — the Gadgil Yojana; self-reliant and self-generating economy; followed by the Plan Holiday (1966-69)
◦ Fourth (1969-74) — growth with stability and self-reliance
◦ Fifth (1974-79) — "Garibi Hatao", poverty removal and self-reliance
◦ Sixth (1980-85) — poverty alleviation and the beginning of economic liberalisation
◦ Twelfth (2012-17) — the last Five Year Plan

 

• The Planning Commission, set up in 1950, was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

 

NOTE

 

• Agriculture and irrigation (Option 1): The focus of the First Five Year Plan.

 

• Poverty alleviation (Option 3): The focus of the Fifth and Sixth Plans.

 

• Export promotion and liberalisation (Option 4): Concerns that came to the fore only with the reforms of 1991.

question: Which Rajput ruler of Amber was the first to enter into a matrimonial alliance with the Mughal emperor Akbar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Raja Bharmal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Raja Bharmal (Bihari Mal) of Amber was the first Rajput ruler to enter into a matrimonial alliance with Akbar, in 1562, when he gave his daughter in marriage to the emperor. (राजा भारमल — 1562, अकबर से वैवाहिक संबंध)

 

• The alliance was the foundation of Akbar's Rajput policy, under which Rajput rulers were treated as allies rather than as subjugated enemies, were given high mansabs and important commands, and retained their ancestral lands as watan jagirs.

 

• The Amber family rose to great eminence in Mughal service. Raja Bhagwan Das, Bharmal's son, and Raja Man Singh, his grandson, both became senior commanders; Man Singh led the Mughal army at the Battle of Haldighati (1576) against Rana Pratap and served as governor of Kabul, Bihar and Bengal.

 

• Mewar under Rana Pratap was the principal Rajput state that refused this accommodation, and the Sisodiyas of Mewar submitted only in 1615, in the reign of Jahangir, when the treaty with Rana Amar Singh restored their territory as a watan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Akbar's other conciliatory measures towards the Rajputs and his non-Muslim subjects: the abolition of the pilgrimage tax in 1563 and of the jizya in 1564, and the promulgation of Sulh-i-Kul, the doctrine of universal peace.

 

• The Battle of Haldighati was fought on 18 June 1576 near Gogunda in Rajasthan; the Mughal army was commanded by Man Singh and Asaf Khan.

 

NOTE

 

• Raja Man Singh (Option 2): Bharmal's grandson and one of Akbar's navratnas, but not the first to make the alliance.

 

• Rana Pratap (Option 3): The ruler of Mewar who resisted Akbar throughout his life and never submitted.

 

• Rana Sanga (Option 4): The ruler of Mewar defeated by Babur at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527, a generation before Akbar.

question: The Unit Trust of India (UTI) was established in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1964.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Unit Trust of India (UTI) was established in 1964 by an Act of Parliament, and was India's first mutual fund. (यूटीआई — 1964, भारत का पहला म्यूचुअल फंड)

 

• It was set up at the initiative of the Reserve Bank of India, which also administered it in its early years, and its purpose was to mobilise the savings of small investors and channel them into the capital market. Its first and best-known scheme was Unit Scheme 1964 (US-64).

 

• In 2003 UTI was bifurcated into the Specified Undertaking of the Unit Trust of India (SUUTI) and UTI Mutual Fund, which is regulated by SEBI.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Years of establishment of major Indian financial institutions, frequently asked together:
◦ Reserve Bank of India — 1935 (nationalised 1949)
◦ Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI) — 1948
◦ Life Insurance Corporation (LIC) — 1956
◦ Unit Trust of India (UTI) — 1964
◦ General Insurance Corporation (GIC) — 1972, commencing business on 1 January 1973
◦ NABARD — 1982, on the recommendation of the Shivaraman Committee
◦ EXIM Bank — 1982; SIDBI — 1990
◦ SEBI — 1988, given statutory status in 1992
◦ IRDAI — 1999

 

• A mutual fund pools the savings of many investors and invests them in securities, spreading risk across a portfolio.

 

NOTE

 

• 1956 (Option 1): The year the Life Insurance Corporation was established and the Second Five Year Plan began.

 

• 1969 (Option 3): The year fourteen major commercial banks were nationalised.

 

• 1982 (Option 4): The year NABARD and the EXIM Bank were established.

question: The Chambal is a tributary of which of the following rivers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yamuna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Chambal is a right-bank tributary of the Yamuna, which it joins near Etawah in Uttar Pradesh. (चंबल — यमुना की सहायक नदी)

 

• It rises from the Janapav hills in the Vindhyan range near Mhow in Madhya Pradesh, flows northward through Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, and is famous for the deep ravines (badlands) it has carved along its course.

 

• Its own tributaries are the Banas, Kali Sindh, Parbati and Shipra. The Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar and Jawahar Sagar dams and the Kota barrage form the Chambal Valley Project, a joint venture of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.

 

• The main tributaries of the Yamuna are the Chambal, Betwa, Ken, Sind, Hindon and Tons. The Yamuna itself rises from the Yamunotri glacier and is the longest tributary of the Ganga, joining it at Prayagraj.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Right-bank tributaries of the Ganga: Yamuna, Son, Punpun and Damodar. Left-bank tributaries: Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Kosi and Mahananda.

 

• The National Chambal Sanctuary, spread over Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, protects the gharial, the Gangetic dolphin and the red-crowned roofed turtle.

 

NOTE

 

• Ganga (Option 1): The Chambal reaches the Ganga only indirectly, through the Yamuna; it is not a direct tributary.

 

• Narmada (Option 2): Flows westward through a rift valley into the Arabian Sea, and has no connection with the Chambal.

 

• Son (Option 4): Itself a right-bank tributary of the Ganga, rising from the Amarkantak plateau.

question: Which instrument is used to measure the depth of the ocean?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fathometer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A fathometer is used to measure the depth of the ocean. (गहराईमापी)

 

• It works on the principle of echo sounding — a pulse of ultrasound is sent downward from the ship, and the time taken for the echo to return from the sea bed is measured. Since the speed of sound in sea water is known (about 1,500 m/s), the depth is calculated as:
◦ Depth = (speed of sound × time) ÷ 2, the division by two being necessary because the sound travels down and back.

 

• The same principle underlies SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging), which is used to detect submarines, shoals of fish and submerged objects. The unit fathom equals 6 feet or about 1.8 metres.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Instruments and the quantities they measure, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Altimeter — altitude or height above sea level
◦ Odometer — distance travelled by a vehicle
◦ Speedometer — speed of a vehicle
◦ Manometer — pressure of a gas
◦ Barometer — atmospheric pressure
◦ Hygrometer — humidity
◦ Anemometer — wind speed
◦ Lactometer — purity of milk
◦ Hydrometer — density of liquids
◦ Seismograph — intensity of earthquakes
◦ Pyrometer — very high temperatures
◦ Salinometer — salinity of sea water

 

NOTE

 

• Altimeter (Option 1): Measures height above sea level, and is used in aircraft — the reverse of measuring depth.

 

• Odometer (Option 3): Records the distance covered by a vehicle.

 

• Manometer (Option 4): Measures the pressure of a gas in a closed vessel.

question: Which instrument is used to record the electrical activity of the human heart?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Electrocardiograph.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An electrocardiograph is the instrument used to record the electrical activity of the heart, and the record it produces is called an electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG). (हृदय की विद्युतीय गतिविधि का अभिलेखन)

 

• It is used to detect arrhythmias, heart attacks (myocardial infarction) and other disorders of the heart's rhythm and conduction.

 

• Facts about the human heart frequently asked alongside: it is about the size of a clenched fist, weighs roughly 300 grams, has four chambers — two atria and two ventricles — and beats about 72 times a minute at rest. It is enclosed in a double membrane called the pericardium, and the sino-atrial (SA) node is its natural pacemaker.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Medical instruments and their uses:
◦ Electroencephalograph (EEG) — electrical activity of the brain
◦ Sphygmomanometer — blood pressure
◦ Stethoscope — listening to the sounds of the heart and lungs; invented by René Laennec
◦ Endoscope — examining internal organs; works on total internal reflection through optical fibres
◦ Thermometer — body temperature
◦ Dialysis machine — filtering the blood when the kidneys fail
◦ Pacemaker — regulating the heartbeat by electrical impulses

 

• The first successful human heart transplant was performed by Dr. Christiaan Barnard in South Africa in 1967.

 

NOTE

 

• Electroencephalograph (Option 1): Records the activity of the brain, not the heart — the commonest confusion in this question.

 

• Stethoscope (Option 3): Allows a physician to hear the heartbeat, but produces no recording of its electrical activity.

 

• Endoscope (Option 4): Used to look inside the body through a natural opening or a small incision.

question: Which Gupta ruler bore the title 'Kaviraja' and is depicted playing the veena on his coins?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Samudragupta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Samudragupta (335-375 CE) bore the title "Kaviraja", the king among poets, and is shown playing the veena on his coins, which testifies to his accomplishment in music. (समुद्रगुप्त — कविराज, वीणावादक)

 

• His achievements are recorded in the Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayag Prashasti), composed in Sanskrit by his court poet Harisena and engraved on an Ashokan pillar. It describes his conquests in Aryavarta (the north, where kings were uprooted) and Dakshinapatha (the south, where kings were defeated and reinstated as tributaries).

 

• For the range of his conquests the historian V.A. Smith called him the "Napoleon of India". He performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and issued coins of eight types, including the Ashvamedha, Tiger-slayer, Archer and Veena-player types.

 

• He was a devotee of Vishnu but tolerant of other faiths; the Sri Lankan king Meghavarna is said to have obtained his permission to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other Gupta rulers and their distinctions:
◦ Chandragupta I (319-335 CE) — the first great Gupta ruler; married Kumaradevi of the Lichchhavis; the Gupta Era is dated from 319-320 CE
◦ Chandragupta II (375-415 CE) — titles Vikramaditya and Simhavikrama; defeated the Shakas; the Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited India in his reign; his court is traditionally said to have had the navratnas, including Kalidasa
◦ Kumaragupta I — founded Nalanda University
◦ Skandagupta — repelled the Huna invasions; repaired the Sudarshana lake in Kathiawar

 

• The Gupta period is often called the Golden Age of India for its achievements in literature, art, science and mathematics — Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta belong to this era or shortly after.

 

NOTE

 

• Chandragupta I (Option 1): The founder of Gupta greatness, but not associated with the title Kaviraja.

 

• Chandragupta II (Option 3): Known as Vikramaditya; his coins show him as an archer and lion-slayer, not a musician.

 

• Skandagupta (Option 4): Remembered chiefly for his defence against the Hunas.

question: Which Article of the Constitution of India deals with the definition of a Money Bill?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 110.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Article 110 of the Constitution defines a Money Bill. (अनुच्छेद 110 — धन विधेयक की परिभाषा)

 

• A Bill is deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with the imposition or regulation of a tax, the borrowing of money by the Government, the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund, the appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund, declaring an expenditure to be charged on that Fund, or the receipt and audit of money on behalf of the Government.

 

• Key features of a Money Bill:
◦ It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the recommendation of the President.
◦ The Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject it; it may only make recommendations, and must return the Bill within 14 days.
◦ If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, it is deemed to have been passed by both Houses.
◦ There is no provision for a joint sitting on a Money Bill.
◦ The decision of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related Articles of Parliament worth remembering:
◦ Article 107 — provisions as to the introduction and passing of Bills
◦ Article 108 — joint sitting of both Houses
◦ Article 109 — special procedure in respect of Money Bills
◦ Article 111 — assent of the President to Bills
◦ Article 112 — the Annual Financial Statement (Budget)
◦ Article 114 — Appropriation Bills
◦ Article 117 — special provisions as to Financial Bills
◦ Article 266 — the Consolidated Fund and the Public Account; Article 267 — the Contingency Fund

 

• Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.

 

NOTE

 

• Article 108 (Option 1): Provides for a joint sitting of the two Houses, which may be summoned in a deadlock over an ordinary Bill — but never over a Money Bill.

 

• Article 112 (Option 3): Deals with the Annual Financial Statement, the Budget.

 

• Article 115 (Option 4): Deals with supplementary, additional or excess grants.

question: 'Yakshagana', a traditional dance-drama combining dance, music and dialogue, belongs to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Yakshagana is a traditional dance-drama of Karnataka, performed chiefly in the coastal districts of the state. (यक्षगान — कर्नाटक)

 

• It combines dance, music, spoken dialogue, elaborate costumes and stage technique, and its themes are drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Puranas. Performances traditionally begin in the evening and continue through the night.

 

• The performers wear towering headgear (kirita), brilliant costumes and heavy face paint. The troupe is led by the Bhagavata, who sings the narrative and conducts the performance, accompanied by the chande and maddale drums.

 

• Dr. Shivaram Karanth, who received the Jnanpith Award, did much to revive and modernise the form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Traditional theatre and dance-drama forms of India:
◦ Kerala — Koodiyattam (the oldest surviving Sanskrit theatre, a UNESCO Intangible Heritage), Krishnattam, Theyyam, Theeyattu, Mudiyettu, Chakyar Koothu
◦ Tamil Nadu — Therukoothu, Bhagavata Mela
◦ Andhra Pradesh — Veedhi Natakam, Burrakatha
◦ Maharashtra — Tamasha, Dashavatar
◦ Gujarat — Bhavai
◦ West Bengal — Jatra
◦ Uttar Pradesh — Nautanki, Ramlila, Raslila
◦ Punjab — Swang; Rajasthan — Khyal, Rammat
◦ Assam — Ankiya Nat, associated with Srimanta Sankardeva

 

NOTE

 

• Kerala (Option 2): Home of Kathakali, Koodiyattam and Theeyattu, all distinct from Yakshagana.

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 3): Known for Therukoothu and the classical Bharatanatyam.

 

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 4): Known for Kuchipudi and the ballad form Burrakatha.

question: The 'Nongkrem' dance festival is celebrated by which tribe of Meghalaya?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khasi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ka Pomblang Nongkrem, popularly called the Nongkrem dance festival, is celebrated by the Khasi tribe of Meghalaya. (नोंगक्रेम — खासी जनजाति, मेघालय)

 

• It is a five-day thanksgiving festival held in autumn at Smit, the capital of the Khyrim Syiemship near Shillong, to thank the goddess Ka Blei Synshar for a good harvest and to pray for peace and prosperity.

 

• Its central rite is the Pomblang, or goat sacrifice, offered by the Syiem (the chief) of Khyrim. Unmarried girls in gold and silver ornaments and men bearing swords and whisks perform the dance.

 

• Meghalaya has three principal tribes — the Khasi, the Garo and the Jaintia — and all three follow a matrilineal system of descent and inheritance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other festivals of Meghalaya:
◦ Wangala — the hundred-drum harvest festival of the Garo tribe, in honour of the sun god Saljong
◦ Shad Suk Mynsiem — the spring dance of the Khasis, meaning "dance of the joyful heart"
◦ Behdienkhlam — the principal festival of the Jaintia tribe
◦ Laho dance — of the Jaintias
◦ Strawberry Festival and the Cherry Blossom Festival — modern additions

 

• Meghalaya, meaning "the abode of clouds", became a full state in 1972. Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (Sohra) are among the wettest places on earth, and Mawlynnong is called Asia's cleanest village.

 

NOTE

 

• Garo (Option 2): Celebrates Wangala, the hundred-drum festival.

 

• Bodo (Option 3): A tribe of Assam, which celebrates Baishagu.

 

• Mizo (Option 4): The principal tribe of Mizoram, which celebrates Chapchar Kut.

question: Which of the following is an example of a contact force?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Frictional force.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Frictional force is a contact force, because it acts only when two surfaces are physically in contact with each other. (घर्षण बल — संपर्क बल)

 

• Forces are of two kinds:
◦ Contact forces — which require physical contact: frictional force, muscular force, normal reaction, tension in a string, air resistance and buoyant force
◦ Non-contact forces (field forces) — which act at a distance without contact: gravitational force, magnetic force and electrostatic force

 

• Friction always acts in a direction opposite to the direction of relative motion between the surfaces. Its order of magnitude is static friction > sliding friction > rolling friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings are used to reduce it.

 

• Friction is often called a "necessary evil" — it wears out machinery and wastes energy as heat, but without it we could neither walk nor write, and vehicles could neither move nor stop.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The four fundamental forces of nature are the gravitational force, the electromagnetic force, the strong nuclear force (the strongest of all, which binds the nucleus) and the weak nuclear force.

 

• Methods of reducing friction: lubricants such as oil and grease, ball bearings, polishing surfaces, and streamlining the shape of vehicles, aircraft and ships.

 

NOTE

 

• Gravitational force (Option 1): A non-contact force; it acts between all bodies having mass, however far apart they may be.

 

• Magnetic force (Option 2): A non-contact force, acting through a magnetic field.

 

• Electrostatic force (Option 4): A non-contact force between charged bodies, described by Coulomb's law.

question: The Linguistic Survey of India was conducted under the direction of which scholar?
solution_text:
The correct answer is George Abraham Grierson.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Linguistic Survey of India (LSI) was conducted under the direction of Sir George Abraham Grierson, an Irish civil servant and linguist of the Indian Civil Service. (भारतीय भाषा सर्वेक्षण — जॉर्ज अब्राहम ग्रियर्सन)

 

• The survey was launched in 1894 and its findings were published in eleven volumes between 1903 and 1928. It recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects, and remains the most comprehensive survey of Indian languages ever undertaken.

 

• Grierson classified the languages of India into families and gave a specimen passage — usually the parable of the Prodigal Son — in each, which made comparison possible. He was knighted in 1912.

 

• The New Linguistic Survey of India was later taken up, and the People's Linguistic Survey of India (PLSI), a non-official effort led by Ganesh Devy, was published from 2010 onwards.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's four principal language families: Indo-Aryan (about 78% of speakers), Dravidian (about 20%), Sino-Tibetan and Austro-Asiatic. Andamanese is sometimes counted as a fifth.

 

• The Eighth Schedule contains 22 languages. Census 2011 recorded 121 languages and 270 mother tongues with more than 10,000 speakers.

 

• The Scheme for Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages (SPPEL) works for languages spoken by fewer than 10,000 people, and is coordinated by the Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru.

 

NOTE

 

• Sir William Jones (Option 1): Founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 and propounded the common origin of Sanskrit, Greek and Latin.

 

• Max Muller (Option 3): The German scholar who edited the Rigveda and the Sacred Books of the East series.

 

• James Prinsep (Option 4): Deciphered the Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts in 1837.

question: The Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR), the predecessor of ISRO, was set up in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1962.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) was set up in 1962 by the Department of Atomic Energy, under the chairmanship of Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, who is regarded as the father of the Indian space programme. (इनकॉस्पार — 1962)

 

• INCOSPAR established the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) near Thiruvananthapuram, chosen because it lies close to the magnetic equator. India's first sounding rocket was launched from Thumba on 21 November 1963.

 

• INCOSPAR was reorganised as the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on 15 August 1969, and the Department of Space was established in 1972, bringing ISRO under it.

 

• Milestones of the Indian space programme: Aryabhata (1975), India's first satellite, launched from the Soviet Union; Rohini (1980), the first satellite placed in orbit by an Indian launch vehicle, the SLV-3; Chandrayaan-1 (2008); Mangalyaan (2013); Chandrayaan-3 (2023); and Aditya-L1 (2023).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• ISRO's headquarters is at Bengaluru. Its major centres are the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (launch vehicles) at Thiruvananthapuram, the U R Rao Satellite Centre at Bengaluru, the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota, the Space Applications Centre at Ahmedabad and the National Remote Sensing Centre at Hyderabad.

 

• 23 August is observed as National Space Day, marking the soft landing of Chandrayaan-3 near the lunar south pole in 2023.

 

NOTE

 

• 1969 (Option 2): The year ISRO itself was formed, on 15 August.

 

• 1972 (Option 3): The year the Department of Space and the Space Commission were established.

 

• 1975 (Option 4): The year India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Santhali language?

I. It is written in the Ol Chiki script.

II. It belongs to the Austro-Asiatic family of languages.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (संताली — ओल चिकी लिपि, ऑस्ट्रो-एशियाटिक परिवार)

 

• Statement I is correct: Santhali is written in the Ol Chiki script, devised in 1925 by Pandit Raghunath Murmu. Before this the language was written in Bengali, Odia, Devanagari or Roman characters.

 

• Statement II is correct: Santhali belongs to the Austro-Asiatic (Munda) family of languages, and is the only language of that family included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.

 

• Santhali is spoken chiefly in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar and Assam by the Santhal community, the largest tribal group in eastern India. It was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, along with Bodo, Dogri and Maithili.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Santhal Rebellion (Santhal Hul) of 1855-56 was led by the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu against moneylenders, zamindars and the colonial administration. It led to the creation of the Santhal Parganas as a separate district in 1856.

 

• Languages of the Eighth Schedule and their families: Bodo and Manipuri are Sino-Tibetan; Santhali is Austro-Asiatic; Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam are Dravidian; the remaining fifteen are Indo-Aryan.

 

• Toda, spoken in the Nilgiris, is an endangered Dravidian language of a very different kind, and is not in the Eighth Schedule.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: Which disease was declared to have been eradicated worldwide by the World Health Organization in 1980?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Smallpox.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide by the World Health Organization in 1980. It remains the only human disease ever to have been eradicated. (चेचक — 1980 में विश्व से उन्मूलित घोषित)

 

• The disease was caused by the variola virus. The vaccine against it was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, using material from cowpox — the origin of the very word "vaccine", from the Latin *vacca*, a cow. Jenner is called the father of immunology.

 

• The last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977. India was declared smallpox-free in 1977.

 

• The only other disease to have been eradicated is rinderpest, a disease of cattle, declared eradicated in 2011.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948, and its headquarters is at Geneva, Switzerland. 7 April is observed as World Health Day.

 

• India was certified polio-free by the WHO in 2014, along with the rest of the South-East Asia Region. The last case of wild poliovirus in India was reported in January 2011 in West Bengal. The Pulse Polio Programme was launched in 1995.

 

• Diseases and their causes frequently asked: smallpox, polio, measles, dengue, rabies and AIDS are viral; tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, tetanus and leprosy are bacterial; malaria and kala-azar are caused by protozoa.

 

NOTE

 

• Poliomyelitis (Option 1): Not yet eradicated globally, though India has been polio-free since 2014.

 

• Malaria (Option 3): Caused by the Plasmodium parasite and transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito; still widely prevalent.

 

• Tuberculosis (Option 4): Caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*; India aims to eliminate it under the National TB Elimination Programme.

question: The 'Sonepur Mela', regarded as Asia's largest cattle fair, is held in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bihar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sonepur Mela, also called the Harihar Kshetra Mela, is held at Sonepur in the Saran district of Bihar, at the confluence of the Ganga and the Gandak. It is regarded as Asia's largest cattle fair. (सोनपुर मेला — बिहार)

 

• It begins on Kartik Purnima and continues for about a fortnight, sometimes for a month. Elephants, horses, cattle, camels, birds and dogs are traded there, and it is famous for its elephant bazaar, though the trade in elephants is now prohibited by law.

 

• The fair is said to date back to ancient times, and the Harihar Nath temple nearby is associated with the legend of Gaja and Graha, the elephant and the crocodile.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Famous fairs and their locations, frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Pushkar Fair — Rajasthan; a camel and livestock fair held on Kartik Purnima
◦ Nagaur Fair — Rajasthan; second largest cattle fair in India
◦ Kumbh Mela — held by rotation at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik
◦ Ambubachi Mela — Kamakhya, Assam
◦ Gangasagar Mela — West Bengal
◦ Surajkund Crafts Mela — Haryana
◦ Hemis Festival — Ladakh
◦ Chandrabhaga Fair — Jhalrapatan, Rajasthan

 

• Ima Keithel at Imphal, Manipur, is a market run entirely by women and is often called the "mother's market".

 

NOTE

 

• Uttar Pradesh (Option 2): Hosts the Magh Mela and Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj and the Taj Mahotsav at Agra.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Hosts the Pushkar and Nagaur cattle fairs.

 

• West Bengal (Option 4): Hosts the Gangasagar Mela at Sagar Island.

question: The headquarters of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is located in which city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jakarta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The headquarters of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is at Jakarta, Indonesia. (आसियान — जकार्ता, इंडोनेशिया)

 

• ASEAN was established on 8 August 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration, signed by its five founding members — Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined later, bringing the membership to ten.

 

• Its motto is "One Vision, One Identity, One Community", and its objectives are to accelerate economic growth, social progress and cultural development, and to promote regional peace and stability.

 

• India is not a member but a dialogue partner since 1996, and the two sides have a Free Trade Agreement in goods (2009) and a strategic partnership. India's Act East Policy, which replaced the Look East Policy in 2014, places ASEAN at its centre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Headquarters of other regional and international organisations:
◦ SAARC — Kathmandu, Nepal; established at Dhaka in 1985 with seven members, Afghanistan joining in 2007
◦ BIMSTEC — Dhaka, Bangladesh
◦ European Union — Brussels
◦ African Union — Addis Ababa
◦ OPEC — Vienna; UNIDO and IAEA — Vienna
◦ Commonwealth — London
◦ Shanghai Cooperation Organisation — Beijing

 

NOTE

 

• Bangkok (Option 2): The city where the Bangkok Declaration founding ASEAN was signed in 1967, and the headquarters of UNESCAP — but not the seat of the ASEAN Secretariat.

 

• Manila (Option 3): Headquarters of the Asian Development Bank.

 

• Singapore (Option 4): A founding member of ASEAN and the venue of the Shangri-La Dialogue.

question: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, the national mission for financial inclusion, was launched in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2014.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on 28 August 2014 as the National Mission for Financial Inclusion. (पीएमजेडीवाई — 2014)

 

• Its object is to ensure affordable access to banking accounts, remittances, credit, insurance and pension for every household. Its guiding slogan is "Mera Khata — Bhagya Vidhata".

 

• Its principal features:
◦ A zero-balance basic savings bank deposit account, with no minimum balance requirement
◦ A RuPay debit card carrying accident insurance cover of ₹2 lakh for cards issued after 28 August 2018 (₹1 lakh for earlier cards)
◦ Life insurance cover of ₹30,000 for eligible accounts opened in the first year
◦ An overdraft facility of up to ₹10,000 after satisfactory operation of the account

 

• PMJDY entered the Guinness World Records for the greatest number of bank accounts opened in a week during its inaugural week.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The JAM trinity — Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile — forms the backbone of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), which reduces leakage in subsidy payments.

 

• Other social security schemes launched in 2015: Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) and the Atal Pension Yojana (APY).

 

• The Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) on comprehensive financial services recommended measures that led to the creation of Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks.

 

NOTE

 

• 2012 (Option 1), 2016 (Option 3) and 2018 (Option 4) are incorrect. Note that 2016 was the year of demonetisation and of the launch of the BHIM app, and 2018 the year the accident cover under PMJDY was raised to ₹2 lakh.

question: Who is the author of the novel 'Untouchable', first published in 1935?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mulk Raj Anand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Untouchable" (1935) was written by Mulk Raj Anand. It describes a single day in the life of Bakha, a young sweeper, and is among the earliest Indian novels in English to deal directly with caste and untouchability. (अनटचेबल — मुल्कराज आनंद)

 

• The preface to the novel was written by E.M. Forster. Anand's other well-known works are "Coolie" (1936), "Two Leaves and a Bud" (1937), "The Village", "The Big Heart" and "Private Life of an Indian Prince".

 

• He is grouped with R.K. Narayan and Raja Rao as one of the "trinity" of early Indian writing in English, and was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1968.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major early Indian novelists in English and their works:
◦ R.K. Narayan — "Swami and Friends", "The Guide" (Sahitya Akademi Award, 1960), "The Painter of Signs", "The Man-Eater of Malgudi"; creator of the fictional town of Malgudi
◦ Raja Rao — "Kanthapura", "The Serpent and the Rope" (Sahitya Akademi Award)
◦ Bhabani Bhattacharya — "So Many Hungers!", "He Who Rides a Tiger"
◦ Khushwant Singh — "Train to Pakistan"
◦ Kamala Markandaya — "Nectar in a Sieve"

 

NOTE

 

• Raja Rao (Option 2): Author of "Kanthapura", a novel of the freedom movement in a South Indian village.

 

• R.K. Narayan (Option 3): Author of "The Guide" and "The Painter of Signs", set in Malgudi.

 

• Bhabani Bhattacharya (Option 4): Author of "So Many Hungers!", on the Bengal famine of 1943.

question: International volleyball is governed by which of the following bodies?
solution_text:
The correct answer is FIVB.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• International volleyball is governed by the Fédération Internationale de Volleyball (FIVB), founded in 1947 and headquartered at Lausanne, Switzerland. (एफआईवीबी — अंतर्राष्ट्रीय वॉलीबॉल महासंघ)

 

• Volleyball was invented in 1895 by William G. Morgan in the United States, and became an Olympic sport at Tokyo in 1964.

 

• Rules of the game: each team has six players on court; a set is played to 25 points and must be won by a margin of two; a match is the best of five sets, the deciding fifth set being played to 15 points. The court measures 18 m × 9 m, and the net is 2.43 m high for men and 2.24 m for women.

 

• Common terms: serve, spike, block, dig, set, libero, ace and deuce.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Governing bodies of major sports:
◦ FIFA — football; Zurich, Switzerland; founded 1904
◦ FIBA — basketball; Mies, Switzerland
◦ FIH — hockey; Lausanne, Switzerland
◦ ICC — cricket; Dubai, UAE
◦ BWF — badminton; Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
◦ ITF — tennis; London
◦ World Athletics — Monaco
◦ FIDE — chess; Lausanne
◦ IOC — Lausanne, Switzerland

 

• The Volleyball Federation of India is the national body, and the Prime Volleyball League is India's professional competition.

 

NOTE

 

• FIBA (Option 2): Governs basketball, a game of five players a side.

 

• FIFA (Option 3): Governs football.

 

• FIH (Option 4): Governs hockey.

question:
Which of the following is/are events included in the Decathlon?

I. Pole vault

II. Marathon
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Only Statement I is correct. (डेकाथलॉन में पोल वॉल्ट सम्मिलित है, मैराथन नहीं)

 

• Statement I is correct: the pole vault is one of the ten events of the Decathlon.

 

• Statement II is incorrect: the marathon, run over 42.195 km, is not part of the Decathlon. The longest running event in the Decathlon is the 1500 metres.

 

• The Decathlon is a men's combined event of ten disciplines held over two days:
◦ Day 1 — 100 m, long jump, shot put, high jump, 400 m
◦ Day 2 — 110 m hurdles, discus throw, pole vault, javelin throw, 1500 m

 

• The corresponding women's event is the Heptathlon, of seven events: 100 m hurdles, high jump, shot put, 200 m, long jump, javelin throw and 800 m.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Athletics events are grouped as track events (sprints, middle and long distance, hurdles, relays, walks), field events (jumps and throws) and combined events (Decathlon, Heptathlon, Pentathlon).

 

• The four throwing events are the shot put, discus, javelin and hammer; the four jumping events are the long jump, triple jump, high jump and pole vault.

 

• Athletics is governed by World Athletics, formerly the IAAF, founded in 1912 and headquartered at Monaco. Neeraj Chopra won India's first Olympic gold in athletics in the javelin throw at Tokyo 2020.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 is incorrect because the pole vault is unquestionably a Decathlon event.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect because the marathon is a standalone road race, not part of any combined event.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect because Statement I is correct.

question: Which school of ancient Indian art, patronised by the Satavahanas, is known for its use of white marble and for depicting scenes from the life of the Buddha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Amaravati school.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Amaravati school of art flourished in the lower Krishna-Godavari valley of present-day Andhra Pradesh, under the patronage of the Satavahanas and later the Ikshvakus. (अमरावती कला शैली — सातवाहन काल)

 

• Its distinguishing features:
◦ The use of white marble (a whitish-green limestone), in contrast to the grey schist of Gandhara and the red sandstone of Mathura
◦ Narrative panels depicting scenes from the life of the Buddha and the Jataka stories
◦ Slender, graceful figures shown in vigorous movement, with a marked sense of drama and crowded composition

 

• It was an indigenous school, entirely free of Greek influence, and its chief site is the Mahachaitya (Great Stupa) at Amaravati. Its influence spread to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three great schools of art of the early centuries CE:
◦ Gandhara school — north-west India, under the Kushanas; a blend of Greek and Indian styles, hence "Greco-Buddhist"; grey schist; wavy hair, muscular bodies and realistic drapery; patronised chiefly by Kanishka
◦ Mathura school — Uttar Pradesh, under the Kushanas; red sandstone from Sikri; entirely indigenous; produced images of the Buddha, and also Jain and Brahmanical figures; the first headless statue of Kanishka comes from Mathura
◦ Amaravati school — Andhra Pradesh, under the Satavahanas; white marble; narrative panels

 

• The first images of the Buddha in human form were produced almost simultaneously by the Gandhara and Mathura schools; before this, the Buddha had been represented only by symbols such as the lotus, the wheel, the Bodhi tree and the stupa.

 

NOTE

 

• Gandhara school (Option 1): The Greco-Buddhist school of the north-west, using grey schist.

 

• Mathura school (Option 2): An indigenous school using red sandstone.

 

• Sarnath (Option 4): A great centre of Buddhist art in the Gupta period, and the site of the Ashokan Lion Capital, but not a distinct school of the Satavahana age.

question: 'Sattriya', one of the eight classical dance forms of India, is associated with the monasteries of which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Assam.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sattriya is the classical dance form of Assam, and takes its name from the Sattras — the Vaishnava monasteries of the state, in which it has been preserved for centuries. (सत्रीया — असम)

 

• It was created in the fifteenth century by the saint-reformer Srimanta Sankardeva as part of the Ekasarana Naam Dharma or Neo-Vaishnavite movement, and was used as a medium of religious instruction through the dance-drama form Ankiya Nat.

 

• It was traditionally performed by male monks (bhokots) within the monasteries. It was recognised as a classical dance form by the Sangeet Natak Akademi in 2000, the most recent addition to the classical canon.

 

• Its accompaniment includes the khol (a drum), taal (cymbals) and the flute, and its music is called Borgeet, composed by Sankardeva and Madhavdeva.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The eight classical dance forms of India and their states:
◦ Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu
◦ Kathak — Uttar Pradesh
◦ Kathakali and Mohiniyattam — Kerala
◦ Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh
◦ Odissi — Odisha
◦ Manipuri — Manipur
◦ Sattriya — Assam

 

• All of them derive their theoretical basis from the Natyashastra of Bharata Muni.

 

• The Majuli island in the Brahmaputra, the largest river island in the world, is the principal centre of the Sattra institutions.

 

NOTE

 

• Odisha (Option 2): Home of Odissi, associated with the temples and the Maharis and Gotipuas.

 

• Manipur (Option 3): Home of Manipuri, best known for its Raas Leela.

 

• Sikkim (Option 4): Known for the Singhi Chham and Chham monastic dances, which are folk and ritual forms rather than classical ones.

question: Who was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Annie Besant.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Annie Besant became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress, presiding over the Calcutta Session of 1917. (एनी बेसेंट — कांग्रेस की प्रथम महिला अध्यक्ष, 1917)

 

• She was an Irishwoman who came to India in 1893 and led the Theosophical Society after the death of Colonel Olcott. She founded the Central Hindu College at Banaras, which later grew into the Banaras Hindu University, and published the newspapers New India and Commonweal.

 

• She launched the Home Rule League in September 1916 at Madras, working alongside Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who had launched his own League in April 1916 at Belgaum. Her internment by the government in 1917 provoked wide protest and was followed by her election as Congress President.

 

• Sarojini Naidu became the first Indian woman President of the Congress, at the Kanpur Session of 1925, and Nellie Sengupta presided at Calcutta in 1933.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Landmark Congress sessions and their Presidents:
◦ 1885, Bombay — the first session, presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee; 72 delegates attended; the Congress was founded by A.O. Hume
◦ 1907, Surat — the split between the Moderates and the Extremists; presided over by Rash Behari Ghosh
◦ 1916, Lucknow — the Lucknow Pact and the reunion of the two groups
◦ 1929, Lahore — Purna Swaraj resolution; presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru
◦ 1938, Haripura — presided over by Subhas Chandra Bose
◦ 1939, Tripuri — Bose re-elected but resigned; Rajendra Prasad took over

 

NOTE

 

• Sarojini Naidu (Option 2): The first Indian woman to be Congress President, in 1925, and the first woman Governor of an Indian state (United Provinces).

 

• Nellie Sengupta (Option 3): An Englishwoman by birth who presided over the Calcutta session of 1933.

 

• Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit (Option 4): The first woman President of the United Nations General Assembly, in 1953, but never President of the Congress.
